old: The suttas repeatedly call nibbāna unestablished or unsupported. Ud 8.1 gives it no coming, going, standing, passing, or arising. SN 12.38 and SN 22.53 tie unestablished consciousness to ending renewed existence. SN 12.64, of all images, uses a beam of light with nowhere to land. Quantum physics likewise says a photon’s state isn’t established as one definite outcome until measured. Saṃsāra is the unestablished becoming established as a definite relational world.
new: The suttas repeatedly call nibbāna unestablished or unsupported. Ud 8.1 says nibbāna has no coming, going, standing, passing, or arising. And then in SN 12.38 and SN 22.53 unestablishing consciousness is what ends renewed existence. Serendipitously, SN 12.64 uses the image of a beam of light that has nowhere to land to describe such unestablished consciousness. And most of us learned in physics 101 that photons don't seem to have one definitive state until they are pinned down by measurement. So now we start to understand that saṃsāra is like that photon, the unestablished flows becoming established or pinned down by interrelating with other flows until they seem to be a solid world.

old: MN 137 tells practitioners to use unification to relinquish diversity, then non-identification to relinquish unity. In MN 121, at every depth of unification the meditator audits the remaining disturbance and finds “just this much – that which depends on oneness.” Unity itself is the last stress.
new: MN 137 gives a two-step recipe. First you use unification (which I'd explain as collecting the mental processes into one attentional direction) to let go of diversity (distraction of the mental processes). Then you use non-identification (not taking anything to be "me") to let go of unity too. In MN 121, at every depth of unification, the meditator checks what disturbance is still left, and tellingly, what they ultimately find is "just this much – that which depends on oneness."

old: Even after the little king or queen fantasy disappears, the mind scurries into a subtler place: “Fine, then I must be the awareness that makes everything real.” But awareness here means something that awares apart from what it awares. Every time someone claims to experience pure awareness (sat chit ananda – being, consciousness, bliss), they can still describe how it feels. So that non-duality is false. What I find instead, and what I believe the Buddha was pointing to, are aware energy flows and the processes that gather them into a self & world.
new: Even after the little king or queen fantasy disappears, the mind scurries into a subtler place: "Fine, then I must be the awareness that makes everything real." But that's just pushing the problem of what is real further down the lane. Now there's something being labeled as awareness, which for some reason is more real than something else, even though the awareness needs the thing it's aware of in order to call itself awareness. And those folks call themselves "non-dualists" in the sense of monism, everything is One (Advaita Vedanta). Clearly, that kind of non-duality is an oxymoron, false on the face of it (like my dad's favorite oxymoron: "military intelligence"). What I find instead, and what I believe the Buddha was pointing to, are aware energy flows and the processes that gather them into a self & world.

new: Iti 44 also shows the limit of nibbāna while you're alive: a living arahant still has preferences and still feels pleasure and pain, although they won't be reborn again, since there's no more craving for existence driving that. So there's no more rebirth ahead, that's a relief. Yet except while in the nibbāna meditation itself, their constructed functioning that can feel pleasure and pain is still running.
